item.description:
FTP and FTPS

  • Eagle Commander connects to FTP and FTPS servers: from ⌘K, or by typing an ftp:// or ftps:// address into the path field. Browsing, F5 both ways, F6, ⇧F6, F7 and F8 work as on SFTP. A large transfer runs on a connection of its own, so the panel stays usable meanwhile.
  • FTPS is encrypted from end to end, or it does not connect. A certificate this Mac does not trust (a NAS, a device) is shown with its fingerprint and asked about once; one that changes later is an error, not a question.
  • Passwords are kept in your keychain under the protocol. A password the server refused is not tried again and again: you are asked, and told why.
  • The server editor (⌘K → New…) asks for the protocol first: SFTP, FTPS or FTP. FTP and FTPS log in with a password. Plain FTP is marked “unencrypted” in the server list, and the editor says what that means.

Servers

  • F6 between two folders on the same SFTP server works now: it is a rename on the server, instant, and nothing goes through your Mac.
  • The progress bar moves smoothly while a large file is copied to or from a server, instead of standing still until the file is done.
  • An error from a server while copying asks "Skip / Skip all / Abort", as on the disk, instead of ending the whole job — and says in plain words what went wrong and with which file, instead of a code from the SSH library.
  • SFTP: when the list of known server keys cannot be read, connecting stops with a message, instead of asking about every server as if it were new.
  • SFTP: that message names the file, too — deleting it starts the list anew, and every server is asked about once more.
  • SFTP: a saved password for a user name that contains “@” (common with hosting) is kept under the whole name. Such a password is asked for once more.
  • ⌘K → Forget Server Key (SFTP) or Forget Certificate (FTPS): after a server was reinstalled, the next connection shows its new key and asks, instead of refusing it.
  • Copying from one server straight to another is refused at once, in plain words, instead of failing file by file.
  • A click selects a row again in the server list (⌘K), the hotlist and the disk list; only the keyboard did. A double click still opens it.
  • ⌘R retries a panel that shows an error, as "Try Again" does.

Names

  • A new name with a “/” is refused also when a combining mark follows it (rename on disk and on SFTP, multi-rename); F7 on SFTP makes such a folder in the right place.
  • Archives: an entry that climbs out of the archive with “..” hidden behind a combining mark is not listed.

Marking

  • ⌘-click marks or unmarks a file, and ⇧-click marks every file from the cursor to the clicked one, as in Finder. A plain click still only moves the cursor, and ⌃-click still opens the context menu.

The mouse

  • F1 opens the list of keyboard shortcuts, as it was meant to; in 1.0 and 1.1 it opened the acknowledgements.
  • In the brief listing (⌘2), a click puts the cursor on the entry clicked and a double click opens it. In every column after the first, both went to the entry in the same row of the first column.
  • The View menu has the full and brief listings and the folder tree, the filter, refreshing, the tabs, swapping and mirroring the panels, and the way to the parent folder, the disk root and the favourites. The Commands menu has the branch of the selected folders and a terminal in the folder under the cursor. The keys stay as they were, yours included. ⌘D is titled Add to or remove from favourites in the menus, as it does both.
  • The context menu of a file starts with Mark or unmark and Select Same Extension, and has Split · join, Unpack, Put the name on the command line (⌃Enter, now also a command for a button or a key of your own) and a terminal in the folder under the cursor. The menu of the folder itself has Deselect All and selecting by mask. The folder tree (⌘3) has a context menu too.
  • The tab row is always there, with a + after the last tab that opens a new one. A tab's context menu opens another, closes it, or locks it to its folder. A new tab keeps the panel's hidden-files, colour and sort settings.
  • The path bar has buttons for the disk root, the favourites and this panel's disks; the status bar has one for the filter, and the open filter field closes with its ×. A click anywhere in the path bar or the status bar, the filter's × included, makes that panel the active one.
  • The command line has a Run button, and a menu of the commands run before that puts the one you pick back into the line. It shows the folder it runs in, the $ and the name of a running command again; all three had shrunk to nothing since 1.0.
  • After a drop, the copy dialog switches between copy and move with a click; before, only the keys held while dropping chose.
  • Find Files: a double click on a hit goes to it.
  • Find Duplicate Files: a click on a file's name or folder ticks it, not only a click on the box.

Quick view

  • ⌃Q turns the other panel into a preview of the file under the cursor — images, PDF, video, documents, anything Quick Look can show — and it follows the cursor. ⌃Q again, or Tab, brings the list back where it was.

Drag and drop

  • Files can be dragged out of a panel — into Finder, Mail, a browser, the other panel — and dropped into one. Grabbing a marked file takes all the marked ones along.

  • ⌥F1 and ⌥F2 list the mounted disks — the startup disk, internal and external drives, disk images, network shares — with their free space, and open the chosen one in the left or the right panel.
  • ⌘E ejects the disk the panel is on. Every panel and tab on it moves to the home folder first, so none is left standing on a disk that is gone.
  • The panel's header shows the free space of its disk, the figure Finder shows.

Renaming

  • The multi-rename window can take the last rename back. Whatever has not changed since gets its old name again; an entry that is gone, or whose old name another file has taken, is named instead of overwritten.

Links

  • ⌃⇧F5 makes a link to the entry under the cursor in the other panel's folder: a symbolic link (absolute, or relative if you move whole trees) or a hard link for a file on the same disk.

The first public release. Everything below arrived in phases 0–15; it is listed here once, by what it does rather than by when it was built.

The panels

  • Two panels with tabs, folder tree, brief and full listings, quick search by name, quick filter, navigation history, favourite folders.
  • Tabs can be locked to a folder: wander off freely, and coming back to the tab brings the folder back with it.
  • Panels side by side or one above the other.
  • Colour rules — mask, age, size, files or folders — with the first matching rule deciding. Marked and hidden entries keep their own colours.
  • The branch (⌃B): every file below the current folder in one flat list, each named by its path, with the ordinary commands working on it.
  • Folder sizes on demand, select by mask, invert, by extension, and a selection that can be put aside and brought back.

Files

  • F5–F8 through a real operation engine: progress, conflicts, cancellation, a background queue, and copyfile(3) on the local disk.
  • Delete to the Trash, delete permanently, or overwrite-then-delete — the last one saying plainly what that is worth on an SSD.
  • Multi-rename with patterns and counters, attributes and timestamps, split and join, checksums (SHA-256, BLAKE3) created and verified.
  • Compare two folders, and synchronize them: a direction per pair, optional deletion of extras, and a verification pass afterwards.
  • Compare two files line by line, with the changed part of a changed line highlighted, encodings, and honest answers for binaries and giants.

Archives

  • ZIP and TAR read and written by us; RAR and 7z read through the system's bsdtar. An archive behaves like a folder in the panel.
  • Encrypted ZIP: ZipCrypto and AES-256 read without ever putting the password on a command line, and packing with AES-256. Passwords live in the session, or in the Keychain if you tick the box.

Finding things

  • Search by name, mask, size, date, content — as text or as a regular expression — optionally inside archives, with locked archives counted rather than silently skipped.
  • Saved searches, and a duplicate finder that decides by content and never offers to select a whole group.

The rest

  • Built-in viewer (text, hex, image) with encodings and search; a command line at the bottom; a real terminal pane below the panels.
  • SFTP: a server behaves like a folder, with the same keys as the disk.
  • A button bar and user commands, and every command rebindable to the key you want.
  • Six languages: English, Slovenian, German, French, Italian, Russian.

Trying, buying, updating

  • Everything works for 30 days. After that the app keeps browsing, searching, viewing, comparing and checksums; copying, moving, deleting and the other commands that change files need a licence — one line above the panels says so, without nagging.
  • A licence is €9.99 once, covers every 1.x version, and is checked on the Mac itself: the key arrives by e-mail, is pasted under Help → Licence…, and works without the internet.
  • Updates through Sparkle: the app asks once whether it may look for them, and never installs one without you.
  • The app sends nothing anywhere — no telemetry, no usage counts — except the update check you agreed to.

Known limits

  • Listing uses FileManager rather than getattrlistbulk(2): correct on SMB and NFS too, but folders past ~20,000 entries show it.
  • No plugins (Total Commander's are Windows DLLs), no FTP or WebDAV, no custom columns or thumbnails, no printing. Each is recorded, with its reason, in docs/faza-15-nacrt.md.
  • Full Disk Access must be granted by hand for ~/Library, other applications' data and Time Machine; macOS offers no way to ask for it. The app says so at first launch and again when a listing is refused.
